fetched_contents.text: Clinical Application of a New Near-Infrared Light-Emitting Diode with Broader Spectrum for Skin Rejuvenation and Hair Growth Enhancement Abstract Background Low-level light therapy (LLLT) and light-emitting diode (LED) therapy have gained popularity in aesthetic dermatology for their effectiveness and convenience in treating skin aging through photobiomodulation (PBM). Recent advancements have led to the development of a new near-infrared (nNIR) LED device with a broader spectrum, aiming to enhance skin rejuvenation and hair growth. This study aims to clinically evaluate the efficacy of this nNIR device. Methods The study included two segments: skin rejuvenation and hair growth evaluation. For skin rejuvenation, 20 participants aged 45–59 used an nNIR LED facial mask for 30 minutes, five times a week over 12 weeks. Parameters such as wrinkle count, skin moisture, elasticity, and density were measured. For hair growth, 25 participants aged 20–55 applied the same device to the scalp daily for 20 weeks, assessing hair growth at 6, 13, and 20 weeks. Results Skin rejuvenation showed significant improvements, with wrinkles decreasing by up to 27.22% and skin texture, elasticity, moisture, and density also improving. Hair growth evaluation indicated a 1.33% increase in hair count by 20 weeks, with high participant satisfaction and no adverse reactions reported. Conclusion The nNIR LED device demonstrated clinical efficacy in skin rejuvenation and hair growth, highlighting the benefits of a broader spectral range in PBM. While further research with larger and more diverse populations is recommended, this nNIR LED device suggests significant potential for advancements in aesthetic treatments. Level of Evidence III This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266. Skin aging is an inevitable biological process characterized by the gradual loss of structural and functional characteristics [1, 2]. In the field of aesthetic dermatology, numerous approaches have been explored to address this condition, which include topical agents, light device, radiofrequency, injectable skin biostimulator, and surgical correction [2]. Among these methods, low-level light therapy (LLLT) and light-emitting diode (LED) therapy have emerged as major approaches and have been widely adopted due to their safety and convenience [3, 4]. These treatments work through photobiomodulation (PBM), where photons emitted by LEDs are absorbed by skin chromophores, resulting in changes in cellular activity, tissue regeneration, repair, and reduced inflammation [5, 6]. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) first documented the therapeutic effects of near-infrared (NIR) light on skin in the 1990s, which subsequently led to the development of devices for skin rejuvenation using infrared radiation [7]. The NIR wavelength range spans from 780 to 2526 nm by the definition of the American Society for Testing and Materials. This NIR region is generally divided into two sub-regions: short wavelength NIR (780–1100 nm) and long wavelength NIR (1100–2526 nm) [8, 9]. Recent LLLT or PBM devices often utilize red and NIR wavelengths, with NIR proving effective for skin rejuvenation and hair growth in the cosmetic LED device market [10, 11]. Advancements in understanding the cascade of non-thermal cell signaling pathways in PBM have significantly increased the efficacy of devices in reducing wrinkles and improving skin texture [12]. Additionally, PBM has been confirmed to be effective for various skin conditions, including alopecia.[13] Several studies have reported the existence of multiple action spectra that can induce PBM within the NIR range, suggesting the potential for increased efficacy with broader spectrum LLLT. [14, 15] To address these prospects, a new near-infrared (nNIR) LED has been developed, which features a broader spectrum than conventional narrow bandwidth NIR chips. This study aims to clinically evaluate the efficacy of this nNIR LED in skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement. For skin evaluation, a total of 20 participants aged between 45 and 59 years, exhibiting eye wrinkles, rough and dry skin, and diminished skin elasticity, were enrolled. Exclusion criteria included individuals using medication known to influence study outcomes, those with skin disorders (e.g., photosensitivity, inflammation, rash, psoriasis, and skin cancer), skin allergies, or sensitivity in the test area, and pregnant or breastfeeding individuals. The nNIR LED device (manufactured and provided by Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.) used in this study is currently classified as a cosmetic beauty device under Korean regulatory standards. After applying exclusion criteria, four individuals were excluded, resulting in a final analysis of 21 participants with a mean age of 37.81 ± 7.76 years. fetched_contents.text: Laser and light-based therapies combined with topical agents for melasma: A systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background: This comprehensive review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of combining laser or light therapy with topical agents for melasma treatment. Methods: A comprehensive search was conducted utilizing PubMed, NCBI, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, Wiley, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. The search aimed to identify pertinent studies from the database’s inception until August 31, 2024. This research encompassed 11 randomized controlled trials including 461 people. The melasma area and severity index and its modified variant (mMASI) were employed for outcome assessment. The Cochrane risk-of-bias tool was used to assess study quality. The GRADE (grading of recommendations assessment, development and evaluation) approach was employed to assess the certainty of evidence. Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness of findings. Data were analyzed using RevMan 5.4.1. Results: Combination therapy demonstrated no significant benefit at 4 weeks, but statistically significant improvements at 8, 12, and 16 weeks (standardized mean difference [SMD]: −0.55; 95% confidence interval: −0.74 to −0.36; P < .00001), indicating a cumulative therapeutic effect. Moderate heterogeneity was observed (I2 = 64%). Sensitivity analysis excluding parallel-design studies (Souza, Bansal, Verma, Qu) confirmed the robustness of efficacy outcomes, with a similar effect size (SMD: −0.45) and reduced heterogeneity (I2 ≈ 41%). Safety analysis showed a significantly higher risk of adverse events in the combination group (OR: 8.96; 95% confidence interval: 3.71–21.64), mainly erythema and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate for efficacy and very low for safety outcomes. Both were judged critically important (importance score 9 and 8, respectively) for clinical decision-making. Conclusion: These findings suggest that combination therapy can effectively enhance melasma treatment. However, careful patient selection and monitoring are crucial due to the risk of side effects. Further large-scale studies with standardized protocols are recommended to validate these findings and optimize treatment strategies. Keywords: efficacy, laser light, melasma, safety, topical agents 1. Introduction Melasma is a common facial skin condition that causes hyperpigmented macules. It is more common in women, especially those with darker skin, and is linked to hormonal fluctuations, sun exposure, and genetics.[1,2] Melasma is caused by melanocyte melanin synthesis, inflammation, and vascular alterations, and can be aggravated by ultraviolet exposure.[3,4] Melasma is characterized by epidermal, dermal, or mixed pigmentation levels, each with specific clinical characteristics and therapeutic needs. This condition is more common in locations with intense sunlight.[4] Melasma can trigger significantly negative physiological and psychological effects. The leading cause of these effects is the chronic and often resistant nature of melasma, which makes it challenging to manage, and can heighten the associated physical and emotional burden.[5,6] Various therapeutic modalities have been developed to treat melasma, including combination treatment that integrates laser- or light-based therapies with topical agents. Melasma laser and light treatments have many advantages over the traditional methods. Intense pulsed light (IPL) and fractional lasers diminish melasma pigmentation. Studies have shown that fractional lasers target melanin deposits and remodel collagen, thereby improving skin texture and tone.[7] Combining laser- or light-based therapies with topical melasma medicines improves the therapeutic efficacy and patient outcomes. Laser therapies, such as fractional laser therapy, target melanin in the skin and reduce pigmentation. fetched_contents.text: Comparison of the efficacy and safety of pulsed dye laser, narrow-band intense pulsed light, and broad-band intense pulsed light in the treatment of erythematotelangiectatic rosacea Abstract Background: Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea (ETR) is a chronic dermatological condition characterized by persistent facial erythema and visible telangiectasia. This study aims to compare the efficacy, safety, and patient satisfaction associated with pulsed dye laser (PDL), narrow-band intense pulsed light (NB-IPL), and broad-band IPL (BB-IPL) in the treatment of ETR. Methods: A total of 112 patients diagnosed with ETR between May 2021 and April 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were divided into three treatment groups: PDL (n = 36), NB-IPL (n = 38), and BB-IPL (n = 38). Treatment outcomes were assessed via VISIA imaging, the Clinical Erythema Assessment (CEA), the Rosacea Quality of Life scale (RosaQoL), and recurrence rates. Pain intensity was measured using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), and skin parameters were analyzed pre- and post-treatment. Correlation analyses were performed to assess associations between treatment modalities, efficacy, and safety profiles. Results: NB-IPL significantly reduced erythema and porphyrin levels compared to PDL and BB-IPL (P < 0.05). BB-IPL showed the most pronounced reduction in sebum levels but was associated with a higher incidence of pigmentation changes. PDL demonstrated comparable efficacy to NB-IPL in reducing erythema while presenting fewer adverse effects. Recurrence rates were low and showed no significant differences among the three groups. Both PDL and NB-IPL demonstrated negative correlations with CEA scores and energy density, whereas NB-IPL showed stronger positive correlations with treatment outcomes and negative associations with sebum levels when compared to BB-IPL. While IPL improves emotional and symptomatic domains in RosaQoL, no significant differences in functional domains were observed. Conclusion: NB-IPL demonstrated superior efficacy in erythema reduction, while BB-IPL effectively reduced sebum production but carried a higher risk of pigmentation. PDL provided a balanced therapeutic profile, combining satisfactory efficacy with fewer adverse events. It affects approximately 1% to 22% of the population across various regions [1]. Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea (ETR) is a subtype that predominantly manifests as persistent facial redness and prominent visible blood vessels, which not only present aesthetic concerns but also impose a significant psychological burden on affected individuals [2]. Although common, the pathophysiology of rosacea remains incompletely understood. Current evidence suggests a multifactorial etiology involving genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, neurovascular dysregulation, and chronic inflammation [3]. Treatment strategies for ETR are diverse, ranging from topical agents to oral medications, and device-based interventions. Among these, laser and light-based therapies have gained prominence due to their ability to directly target the vascular components of the disease, providing both symptomatic relief and cosmetic improvement [4-6]. Pulsed dye laser (PDL) and intense pulsed light (IPL) technologies are particularly notable, as they enable selective photothermolysis of cutaneous chromophores - especially oxyhemoglobin - within superficial blood vessels, thereby diminishing erythema and telangiectasia [7-9]. PDL, a well-established modality in rosacea management, operates within a wavelength range that is preferentially absorbed by hemoglobin, promoting selective photothermolysis of superficial cutaneous vasculature with minimal collateral tissue damage [8,10]. Similarly, IPL delivers non-coherent, broad-spectrum light capable of addressing various dermatological concerns, including vascular lesions. The clinical versatility of IPL is largely attributed to its adjustable parameters, which allow individualized treatment based on patient-specific characteristics and the severity of rosacea. However, its broad wavelength range may lead to non-selective photothermal effects, potentially increasing the risk of adverse events such as post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Technological advancements have led to the development of narrow-band IPL, which focuses energy delivery within a more specific wavelength spectrum to enhance target specificity and minimize adverse effects [9,11]. Despite the clinical promise of these technologies, comparative data on the efficacy and safety of different laser and IPL modalities for treating ETR remain limited. While previous studies have assessed individual modalities, direct head-to-head comparisons are scarce, hindering evidence-based treatment selection tailored to patient-specific needs and therapeutic goals [12,13]. Moreover, evaluating clinical efficacy is crucial, as treatment adherence and patient satisfaction are strongly influenced by both visible improvements and procedural tolerability [14]. fetched_contents.text: Lasers and intense pulsed light (IPL) association with cancerous lesions Abstract The development and use of light and lasers for medical and cosmetic procedures has increased exponentially over the past decade. This review article focuses on the incidence of reported cases of skin cancer post laser or IPL treatment. The existing evidence base of over 25 years of laser and IPL use to date has not raised any concerns regarding its long-term safety with only a few anecdotal cases of melanoma post treatment over two decades of use; therefore, there is no evidence to suggest that there is a credible cancer risk. Although laser and IPL technology has not been known to cause skin cancer, this does not mean that laser and IPL therapies are without long-term risks. Light therapies and lasers to treat existing lesions and CO2 laser resurfacing can be a preventative measure against BCC and SCC tumour formation by removing photo-damaged keratinocytes and encouraged re-epithelisation from stem cells located deeper in the epidermis. A review of the relevant literature has been performed to address the issue of long-term IPL safety, focussing on DNA damage, oxidative stress induction and the impact of adverse events. Keywords: Intense pulsed light (IPL), Actinic keratosis (AK), Ultraviolet (UV), Basal cell carcinoma (BCC), Malignant melanoma (MM)., Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) Introduction The development and use of lasers and light for medical and cosmetic procedures based on the principle of selective photothermolysis [1] has increased exponentially over the past two decades. Since the first commercial cutaneous carbon dioxide laser system became globally available over 40 years ago [2], millions of treatments have taken place often with positive outcomes. This review will look into the research on how light therapies affect cancerous and precancerous skin lesions with the aim of determining whether such treatments could ever initiate cancer or make an existing cancer lesion worse. The notable increase in the cosmetic and medical uses of lasers and IPL systems are not restricted to physicians, as many home-use devices are available with comparable parameters to salon-based equipment [3, 4]. Following the first demonstration of a functional laser device in 1960, it was not until the early 1990s that their use in the medical field became commonplace. Although laser interaction with skin and tissues was investigated from the mid-1960s onwards, the high cost and unreliability of the technology restricted its commercial uptake [5]. In the late 1980s, lasers that targeted specific constituents of tissue, rather than just cutting or ablating, were introduced for the removal of vascular lesions [6, 7]. Throughout the early 1990s, various lasers were introduced for different applications in the dermatology field, ranging from tattoo removal to hair removal. The IPL system is a high power broadband light source as opposed to the monochromatic laser, made its debut in the mid-1990s as an alternative to the available laser sources. The perceived advantages of the IPL were lower cost, less complexity and more flexibility in output parameters along with the incoherent nature of the IPL source compared to the focusing effect on the retina by coherent lasers being generally less hazardous to the eye. Hair removal using monochromatic lasers was initially introduced to the market in the early 1990s [8, 9]. However, in the new millennium, broadband IPL technology emerged as a powerful competitor and challenged the dominance of the laser in the market [10]. A notable reason for the increasing popularity of IPLs amongst dermatologists and beauty therapists is versatility. An IPL system can be configured for different emission spectra by simply varying light filtration. A distinct advantage is the ability to target multiple chromophores over a large skin area in a single pulse compared with narrow beam, small spot size laser systems. Initially, IPLs were utilised for the treatment of vascular malformations such as port wine stains and thread veins. This was because they had the ability to produce longer pulse durations than pulsed dye lasers, the technology most commonly used for vascular treatments, thus allowing larger veins to be targeted and treated. As the 1990s progressed, the use of IPLs became more and more commonplace with photodermatological treatments, with the exception of tattoo removal, being addressed by a wide variety of systems with a myriad of output parameters. IPL-based technology is generally considered a safe procedure as potentially harmful ultraviolet radiation is typically filtered by blocking wavelengths below 500 nm, although there are unwanted effects associated with the treatment. Adverse effects of IPL treatments have been well documented [11]; these include blistering, hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation and if extensive, even scarring. Hyperpigmentation is typically reversible and results from the stimulation of melanin from epidermal melanocytes and is similar to that seen in an ultraviolet light-induced suntan. Hypopigmentation may be permanent and it usually results from thermally induced destruction of melanocytes. A majority of cases occur due to incorrect parameters being selected for the treatment based on the application and patient’s skin colour or ethnicity [12]. Laser and IPL systems all utilise non-ionising radiation; this type of energy does not affect the DNA strands. It is this breakdown of DNA which may lead, in the long term, to cancer. A mini-report on safety, side effects, and clinical limitations

Overall, light-based aesthetic treatments—particularly IPL and lasers—are widely used but carry a mix of acute, long-term, and device-specific risks. The evidence suggests that these technologies are generally safe in routine clinical use, yet they are not without limitations, especially when misapplied or when patients have phototypes that increase vulnerability to adverse effects [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-F4][N5-R4].

Common acute adverse effects include redness, swelling, burns, blisters, and temporary skin discoloration. IPL and laser devices can overheat the skin if settings are improperly chosen, and this can result in burns or blisters that may scar [N5-R2][N5-R3][N7-R3][N7-R4]. In addition, IPL can cause reversible hyperpigmentation or, less commonly, permanent hypopigmentation, especially when parameters are mismatched for the patient’s skin color or ethnicity [N5-F4]. IPL-related oxidative stress and DNA damage have also been noted in the literature, though the evidence base suggests these effects are not clinically catastrophic and are generally less severe than those of ultraviolet radiation [N5-R5][N5-F4].

Longer-term concerns are more nuanced. Although lasers and IPL are not known to cause skin cancer, the long-term safety literature notes that they are not without long-term risks, and some studies have documented rare adverse events and DNA damage concerns [N5-F4]. The same review also notes that IPL can generate reactive oxidative species and DNA damage similar to UV exposure, though the wavelengths commonly used in IPL are generally above the short UV range that is most damaging to DNA [N5-R5][N5-F4]. A separate review on ocular safety found that some IPL goggles provided insufficient protection, which is an important safety concern for practitioners and patients [N7-R1]. This points to a broader limitation: device-specific safety depends on proper use, eye protection, and operator expertise.

Skin types and sensitivity concerns are especially important. IPL is generally considered versatile, but its broad-spectrum nature can make it less predictable in darker skin types. The literature explicitly warns that incorrect parameters can cause post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and that darker skin types are more at risk for PIH and other complications [N5-F4][N5-R1]. IPL devices can also make the skin more vulnerable to ultraviolet rays after treatment, intensifying sensitivity and increasing the risk of complications [N5-R1]. This sensitivity concern is reinforced by the fact that IPL and laser treatments can be used at home or in less regulated settings, where improper application is more common and risk is higher [N7-R3][N7-R4].

Evidence gaps and unmet clinical needs are clear. The safety literature is strong on acute adverse effects and some long-term concerns, but it remains thin on definitive long-term cancer risk, and the evidence base is still considered limited in some comparative studies [N5-F4]. The evidence also shows that treatment outcomes depend heavily on device type, wavelength selection, and patient characteristics, yet standardized protocols are not always uniformly adopted across studies or practices [N5-F4][N4-F3]. For clinical decision-making, safety outcomes in many studies are judged with low certainty, and this matters because side effects can outweigh aesthetic benefits in some cases [N3-F2]. The broader limitation is that while light-based therapies are popular and increasingly accessible, their real-world safety and long-term effects are still best supported by cautious, individualized application rather than one-size-fits-all protocols [N5-F4][N7-R1][N7-R4].
node_outputs.N11:
A mini-report on hyperpigmentation treatment and melasma-specific light-based strategies

Melasma is a chronic, relapsing hyperpigmentation disorder driven by complex interactions among genetic predisposition, hormonal fluctuations, sun exposure, and inflammation [N3-F2]. Age spots are also a broad category of hyperpigmentation, and while the evidence set is less specific to age spots than to melasma, light-based therapies are used clinically for pigmentation concerns, including signs of aging like age spots [N3-R2]. For melasma, the evidence strongly supports combination therapy with topical agents as a more effective strategy than monotherapy [N3-F2].

The best-supported modalities for melasma are laser and light-based therapies combined with topical agents. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials found that combination therapy improved melasma severity and patient satisfaction, with statistically significant improvements at 8, 12, and 16 weeks [N3-F2]. The study also found that combination therapy carried a higher risk of adverse events, mainly erythema and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and it concluded that careful patient selection and monitoring are crucial [N3-F2]. This is an important practical implication: melasma treatment is more effective when combined with topical agents, but the safety profile is more complex, especially because topical ingredients can also influence pigmentation and inflammation [N3-F2].

For age spots, the evidence is less specific than for melasma, but IPL and related light-based treatments are still used clinically for pigmentation and signs of aging [N3-R2]. The same review also notes that red light therapy is popular for skin concerns including signs of aging like wrinkles, age spots, and sagging skin [N3-R2]. However, the evidence for red light therapy as a standalone treatment for age spots is weaker than for combination melasma therapy, and the review emphasizes that the 2024 integrative review on photobiomodulation for melasma included nine relevant studies, suggesting that age spot treatment is not as well-established as melasma in the current evidence base [N3-R5][N3-F2].

Dose, frequency, and combination treatment patterns are important in both conditions. For melasma, combination therapy typically involves fractional laser treatment with topical medications [N3-F2]. The evidence indicates a cumulative therapeutic effect, with improvements starting to appear after 8 weeks and strengthening over time [N3-F2]. In practice, this suggests that treatment is often repeated and that protocols are not limited to a single session. The review also emphasizes that inconsistent treatment protocols, variations in laser parameters, and differences in skin phototypes and topical agents used have led to considerable heterogeneity in outcomes [N3-F2]. This heterogeneity supports the idea that standardized, protocol-driven approaches are needed to optimize results.

Limitations and risks specific to pigmentation disorders are substantial. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is a major concern, and the evidence shows that combination therapy can increase the risk of adverse events, including erythema and PIH [N3-F2]. The same review also reports that some studies showed minimal improvement or even worsening of melasma in darker skin types, especially due to PIH risks [N3-F2]. For age spots, the evidence set is less explicit on risks, but the broader IPL literature warns of reversible hyperpigmentation, permanent hypopigmentation, and skin sensitivity after treatment [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that IPL can make the skin more vulnerable to ultraviolet exposure and intensify sensitivity [N5-R1]. These limitations suggest that pigmentation disorders require cautious, individualized treatment with close monitoring.

In summary, for melasma, the best-supported strategy is laser/light-based therapy combined with topical agents; for age spots, light-based therapies are used clinically but the evidence is less robust than for melasma [N3-F2][N3-R2]. The most important treatment patterns are repeated sessions, combination with topical agents, and careful attention to skin phototype [N3-F2]. The main limitations are post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, PIH, skin sensitivity, and the need for standardized protocols [N3-F2][N5-F4].

A mini-report on current applications of laser, IPL, and LED in aesthetic medicine

Each modality is currently used for a distinct set of aesthetic indications, but their treatment protocols and parameters differ substantially. Laser, IPL, and LED all have broad roles in aesthetic dermatology, but lasers are often used for more targeted chromophore-specific treatments, IPL for broader pigmentation and vascular concerns, and LED for photobiomodulation-based skin rejuvenation and hair growth [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1][N3-R2].

For laser, the evidence emphasizes use in vascular and pigment-related conditions, with particular attention to fractional lasers and other laser systems used in melasma treatment [N3-F2]. The comparative IPL study in rosacea notes that pulsed dye laser, narrow-band IPL, and broad-band IPL are used for vascular concerns and that laser technologies can be tailored to individual patient needs and severity [N4-F3]. In skin rejuvenation, lasers are part of a broader treatment repertoire that includes topical agents, radiofrequency, injectables, and surgery [N1-F1]. In melasma, lasers are combined with topical agents to improve pigmentation and patient satisfaction [N3-F2].

IPL is widely used for skin rejuvenation and pigmentation concerns, including vascular and pigmented lesions. The evidence set shows that IPL is described as a “photo facial” for improving skin color and texture without surgery [N1-R4]. It is also used clinically for skin photoaging and laxity in Asian patients [N1-R5], and the evidence indicates that IPL is often configured for different emission spectra by varying light filtration [N5-F4]. The comparative IPL study in rosacea further explains that IPL delivers non-coherent, broad-spectrum light capable of addressing various dermatological concerns, including vascular lesions, and that narrow-band IPL can improve target specificity [N4-F3]. However, broad-band IPL can carry a higher risk of pigmentation changes, while narrow-band IPL is associated with fewer adverse effects [N4-F3]. This reflects a key protocol difference: IPL treatment parameters are adjusted by wavelength filtering and energy density to match the target condition and patient characteristics [N4-F3].

LED is increasingly used for skin rejuvenation and hair growth. The evidence set states that low-level light therapy and LED therapy have gained popularity in aesthetic dermatology for treating skin aging through photobiomodulation [N1-F1]. A study on a near-infrared LED device showed clinical efficacy in skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement, with improvements in wrinkle count, skin moisture, elasticity, and density after 12 weeks of treatment [N1-F1]. The same study used a broader spectral range and reported no adverse reactions, which suggests that LED can be used in a relatively safe manner in some settings [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that newer LED devices may have broader action spectra that can increase efficacy [N1-F1]. In contrast to lasers and IPL, LED devices are generally considered lower energy and less likely to produce burns or blisters, but their effects are usually slower and more cumulative [N1-F1][N4-R3].

Common indications across the modalities are skin rejuvenation, pigmentation concerns, vascular conditions, and hair growth. Laser is used for vascular and pigment-related conditions, melasma, and skin rejuvenation when combined with topical agents [N3-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1]. IPL is used for skin rejuvenation, pigmentation, vascular lesions, and hair removal [N1-R4][N1-R5][N4-F3]. LED is used for skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement [N1-F1]. For hair removal, the evidence set shows that diode lasers and IPL are both used, with diode lasers generally showing higher efficacy and better comfort in some studies [N8-R1][N8-R2][N8-R3]. This is important because it shows that the same modality can be used across different indications, but the choice of device depends on the condition, skin type, and desired outcome.

Treatment protocols and parameters differ across devices. Lasers are typically chosen for more targeted chromophore-specific treatments and can be adjusted by wavelength, pulse duration, and energy density [N4-F3]. IPL is configured by varying light filtration to target different chromophores and is often used with adjustable energy settings [N5-F4][N4-F3]. LED is generally delivered through photobiomodulation protocols that use specific wavelengths, such as red or near-infrared light, and may be applied continuously over a longer session [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that home-use IPL devices can have similar efficacy and safety to salon-based IPL devices, which reflects a broader trend toward consumer access but also underscores the importance of proper settings and supervision [N4-R2][N7-R3]. In clinical practice, contraindications include photosensitivity, inflammation, skin disorders, skin allergies, and pregnancy/breastfeeding [N1-F1]. For IPL and lasers, darker skin types are especially vulnerable to PIH, and incorrect parameters can cause burns, blisters, hypopigmentation, or hyperpigmentation [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a device-specific approach to treatment, with lasers for targeted vascular/pigment conditions, IPL for broader pigmentation and vascular concerns, and LED for photobiomodulation-based skin rejuvenation and hair growth [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F3].

# Integrated final answer on current applications and recent advancements of light-based therapies in aesthetic medicine

Light-based therapies—including laser, IPL, and LED—are among the most widely used and rapidly evolving tools in aesthetic medicine. They are currently applied to a broad range of indications, from photoaging and skin rejuvenation to pigmentation disorders such as melasma and age spots, and they are increasingly being refined through scientific advances in biological mechanisms, device design, and clinical protocols. The evidence provided across the branch reports shows a clear pattern: these therapies are effective in many settings, but their success depends heavily on device type, patient characteristics, and treatment parameters. Below I integrate the four branch reports into a single coherent assessment.

---

## 1) Current applications of laser, IPL, and LED in aesthetic medicine

### What each modality is used for

Laser, IPL, and LED each have distinct but overlapping applications in aesthetic medicine.

- **Laser** is used for vascular and pigment-related conditions, as well as for skin rejuvenation when combined with topical agents. Lasers are particularly useful for targeting chromophores such as melanin, oxyhemoglobin, and other pigments [N3-F2][N4-F3]. They are also used in hair removal and in melasma treatment, often in combination with topical agents [N3-F2][N8-R1].
  
- **IPL** is widely used for skin rejuvenation, pigmentation concerns, vascular lesions, and hair removal. It is described as a “photo facial” for improving skin color and texture without surgery [N1-R4]. IPL is also used clinically for skin photoaging and laxity, and its broad-spectrum nature allows it to be adapted to different wavelengths and treatment goals [N1-R5][N5-F4].

- **LED** is increasingly used for skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement. Low-level light therapy and LED therapy have gained popularity in aesthetic dermatology for treating skin aging through photobiomodulation [N1-F1]. A study on a near-infrared LED device showed clinical efficacy in skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement, with improvements in wrinkle count, skin moisture, elasticity, and density [N1-F1].

### How treatment protocols and parameters differ across devices

The key difference across these modalities lies in how they deliver energy and how they are adjusted for the target condition.

- **Laser** treatments are typically more targeted and can be adjusted by wavelength, pulse duration, and energy density. This allows for chromophore-specific targeting and can reduce collateral damage [N4-F3]. Lasers are often used for more precise vascular or pigment removal, and their protocols are often more individualized [N4-F3].

- **IPL** is configured by varying light filtration to target different chromophores and is often used with adjustable energy settings. The literature notes that IPL can be configured for different emission spectra, which helps tailor treatment to the patient’s skin and condition [N5-F4][N4-F3]. Narrow-band IPL is associated with better target specificity and fewer adverse effects, while broad-band IPL may be more effective for sebum reduction but carries a higher risk of pigmentation changes [N4-F3].

- **LED** is generally delivered through photobiomodulation protocols and is often applied continuously over longer sessions. The evidence indicates that newer LED devices may have broader action spectra, which can improve efficacy [N1-F1][N6-R4]. LED is generally considered lower energy and less likely to produce burns or blisters than lasers or IPL, but its effects are often slower and more cumulative [N1-F1][N4-R3].

### Common indications and contraindications in practice

The evidence supports a broad set of common indications across the modalities:

- **Skin rejuvenation** and **pigmentation concerns** are among the most common uses for all three modalities [N1-F1][N1-R4][N3-R2].
- **Vascular conditions** are a major application of lasers and IPL [N4-F3].
- **Hair removal** is a prominent use of diode lasers and IPL, with diode lasers often showing better efficacy and comfort in some studies [N8-R1][N8-R2][N8-R3].
- **Hair growth enhancement** is also an emerging indication for LED [N1-F1].

Common contraindications across the modalities include:

- Photosensitivity, inflammation, skin disorders, skin allergies, and pregnancy or breastfeeding [N1-F1].
- For IPL and lasers, darker skin types are especially vulnerable to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) and other complications when parameters are not matched to the patient’s skin color or ethnicity [N5-F4].
- Improper settings can cause burns, blisters, hypopigmentation, or hyperpigmentation [N5-F4][N7-R3].
- Ocular safety is also a concern, with some IPL goggles providing insufficient protection [N7-R1].

In practice, the most common indications are therefore skin rejuvenation, pigmentation concerns, vascular conditions, and hair-related applications, while contraindications are mainly related to skin phototype, inflammation, and improper device settings [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F4][N7-R1].

---

## 2) Recent scientific advances in light-based whitening and brightening

### New biological targets or pathways implicated in light-based whitening

Recent scientific advances suggest that light-based therapies are not just photothermal treatments but also photobiomodulation approaches. The evidence indicates that light can alter cellular activity, tissue regeneration, repair, and inflammation, which supports its use for skin rejuvenation and brightening [N2-R1][N1-F1]. This broader mechanistic view is important because it shifts the discussion from simple “light delivery” to more nuanced biological effects.

The branch reports also emphasize that photobiomodulation can reduce inflammation and improve skin texture, which contributes to a brighter appearance [N2-R1][N2-R5]. For brightening, the evidence points to the role of chromophore absorption and downstream signaling pathways, but the evidence is stronger for general skin rejuvenation than for a single molecular target [N2-R1][N1-F1].

### Recent device or formulation improvements

Recent device improvements have focused on broader spectral ranges and more targeted light delivery.

- A new near-infrared LED device with a broader spectrum was shown to improve skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement, suggesting that broader action spectra may increase efficacy [N1-F1].
- Narrow-band IPL is noted for better target specificity and fewer adverse effects, while broad-band IPL may be more effective for sebum reduction but carries a higher risk of pigmentation changes [N4-F3].
- The literature also points to broader LED devices with enhanced utility and newer aesthetic medical devices, reflecting a trend toward more versatile and effective light-based solutions [N6-R4][N6-R3].
- IPL and other light-based devices are increasingly being used in home settings, with some evidence suggesting that at-home IPL devices can have similar efficacy and safety to salon-based devices [N4-R2][N7-R3].

### Clinical evidence for efficacy and patient outcomes

The clinical evidence is encouraging but heterogeneous.

- For skin rejuvenation, the nNIR LED study reported significant improvements in wrinkle count, skin moisture, elasticity, and density, with no adverse reactions reported [N1-F1].
- For red light therapy, over 90% of patients reported some improvement, including softer and smoother skin, less redness, and lightening of dark spots [N2-R4].
- The evidence for red light therapy as a standalone whitening agent is weaker than for combination melasma therapy, and patient-reported outcomes can be encouraging even when the literature is still evolving [N2-R4][N2-R1].
- The 2024 integrative review on melasma treatment included nine relevant clinical studies, showing that light-based therapy is an active area of research [N3-R5].

Overall, recent scientific advances have improved device design, broader spectral delivery, and biological understanding, but the clinical evidence for standalone whitening remains strongest in skin rejuvenation rather than in isolated brightening protocols [N2-R1][N1-F1][N6-R4].

---

## 3) Hyperpigmentation treatment and melasma-specific light-based strategies

### Which modalities are best supported for melasma and age spots

For **melasma**, the evidence strongly supports **combination therapy** with topical agents. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials found that combination therapy improved melasma severity and patient satisfaction, with statistically significant improvements at 8, 12, and 16 weeks [N3-F2]. The same review concluded that careful patient selection and monitoring are crucial because combination therapy carries a higher risk of adverse events, mainly erythema and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [N3-F2].

For **age spots**, the evidence is less specific than for melasma, but IPL and related light-based treatments are still used clinically for pigmentation and signs of aging [N3-R2]. The evidence set also notes that red light therapy is popular for skin concerns such as wrinkles, age spots, and sagging skin [N3-R2]. However, the evidence for red light therapy as a standalone treatment for age spots is weaker than for melasma, and the literature cautions that outcomes depend on device type, parameters, and patient characteristics [N3-R5][N2-R4].

### Dose, frequency, and combination treatment patterns

The evidence suggests that these conditions respond best to repeated treatment and combination with topical agents.

- For melasma, combination therapy often involves **fractional laser treatment** with topical medications [N3-F2]. The review found a cumulative therapeutic effect, with improvements starting at 8 weeks and strengthening over time [N3-F2].
- For age spots, the evidence indicates that repeated sessions and broader pigmentation-focused light-based approaches are used clinically [N3-R2][N3-R5].
- The literature also emphasizes that inconsistent treatment protocols, variations in laser parameters, and differences in skin phototype and topical agents used have led to considerable heterogeneity in outcomes [N3-F2].

### Limitations and risks specific to pigmentation disorders

The limitations and risks are substantial for pigmentation disorders:

- Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is a major concern, and the evidence shows that combination therapy can increase the risk of adverse events such as erythema and PIH [N3-F2].
- The literature also reports that some studies showed minimal improvement or even worsening of melasma in darker skin types, especially due to PIH risks [N3-F2].
- For IPL and lasers, darker skin types are especially vulnerable to PIH and other complications when parameters are mismatched [N5-F4].
- IPL can also make the skin more vulnerable to ultraviolet exposure and intensify sensitivity [N5-R1].
- The evidence also notes that IPL can cause reversible hyperpigmentation, permanent hypopigmentation, and skin sensitivity after treatment [N5-F4].

In short, for melasma the best-supported strategy is laser/light-based therapy combined with topical agents; for age spots light-based therapies are used clinically but the evidence is less robust than for melasma [N3-F2][N3-R2]. The most important treatment patterns are repeated sessions, combination with topical agents, and careful attention to skin phototype [N3-F2]. The main limitations are post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, PIH, skin sensitivity, and the need for standardized protocols [N3-F2][N5-F4].

---

## 4) Safety, side effects, and clinical limitations

### Common acute and long-term adverse effects

The evidence indicates that light-based aesthetic treatments are generally safe in routine clinical use, but they are not without risks.

- **Acute effects** include redness, swelling, burns, blisters, and temporary skin discoloration [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N7-R3].
- **Longer-term concerns** include oxidative stress, DNA damage, and the possibility of rare adverse events, although the evidence base suggests that these effects are not catastrophic and are generally less severe than those of ultraviolet radiation [N5-R5][N5-F4].
- The evidence also notes that lasers and IPL are not known to cause skin cancer, but they are not without long-term risks, and the literature highlights the need to consider long-term safety carefully [N5-F4].

### Skin types and sensitivity concerns

Skin type is a major factor in safety and efficacy.

- IPL is especially sensitive to skin phototype: incorrect parameters can cause PIH, and darker skin types are at higher risk of PIH and other complications [N5-F4][N5-R1].
- IPL can make the skin more vulnerable to ultraviolet exposure and intensify sensitivity after treatment [N5-R1].
- IPL goggles are sometimes insufficient in real-world use, which increases the risk of ocular injury [N7-R1].
- Lasers and IPL can also be used at home or in less regulated settings, where improper application is more common and risk is higher [N7-R3][N7-R4].

### Evidence gaps and unmet clinical needs

The evidence base is strong on acute adverse effects and some long-term concerns, but gaps remain.

- The long-term cancer risk is still considered limited in the evidence, but the literature notes that the evidence base is still limited in some comparative studies [N5-F4].
- The evidence also shows that treatment outcomes depend on device type, wavelength selection, and patient characteristics, yet standardized protocols are not always uniformly adopted [N5-F4][N4-F3].
- Safety outcomes in many studies are judged with low certainty, which matters because side effects can outweigh aesthetic benefits in some cases [N3-F2].
- A major unmet need is the need for standardized, protocol-driven approaches to reduce heterogeneity and improve reproducibility [N3-F2][N5-F4].

Overall, light-based therapies are popular and increasingly accessible, but their real-world safety and long-term effects are still best supported by cautious, individualized application rather than one-size-fits-all protocols [N5-F4][N7-R1][N7-R4].

---

## 5) Integrated conclusion: what this means for current practice

The current evidence supports the following conclusions:

1. **Laser** is best used for targeted vascular and pigment-related conditions, especially when combined with topical agents for melasma [N3-F2][N4-F3].
2. **IPL** is widely used for skin rejuvenation, pigmentation concerns, vascular lesions, and hair removal, but it is less predictable in darker skin types and carries a higher risk of PIH when parameters are not carefully chosen [N1-R4][N5-F4][N4-F3].
3. **LED** is increasingly used for skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement, with newer devices often having broader spectral ranges and better efficacy [N1-F1][N6-R4].
4. For **melasma**, the strongest evidence supports combination therapy with topical agents; for **age spots**, light-based therapies are used clinically but the evidence is less robust than for melasma [N3-F2][N3-R2].
5. For **skin whitening and brightening**, recent advances focus on photobiomodulation and broader device spectra, but the clinical evidence is strongest for skin rejuvenation rather than standalone brightening protocols [N2-R1][N1-F1][N6-R4].
6. The main safety concerns are burns, blisters, PIH, and UV sensitivity, especially in darker skin types and with improper device use [N5-R1][N5-F4][N7-R1].
7. Evidence gaps remain, particularly in long-term safety and standardized protocols, and the need for careful patient selection and monitoring is clear [N5-F4][N3-F2].

## 6) Practical implications for clinicians and patients

For clinicians, the key takeaway is that light-based therapies should be used in a device-specific, patient-specific way. Lasers and IPL are powerful tools, but their safety and efficacy depend on:

- Correct wavelength selection and energy settings [N4-F3][N5-F4].
- Careful matching to skin phototype and condition [N3-F2][N5-F4].
- Combination with topical agents when appropriate, especially for melasma [N3-F2].
- Close monitoring for adverse effects such as erythema, PIH, and burns [N3-F2][N5-F4].
- Ocular protection and proper device operation, especially with IPL [N7-R1].

For patients, the main message is that light-based therapies can be effective, but they are not universally “safe” in the same way for everyone. Patients should be informed about skin type sensitivity, expected outcomes, and the importance of professional supervision, especially for home-use devices and for darker skin types [N5-F4][N7-R3][N7-R1].

---

## 7) Summary

In summary, light-based therapies—laser, IPL, and LED—are currently among the most important tools in aesthetic medicine for photoaging, skin rejuvenation, pigmentation disorders, and hair-related concerns. Recent scientific advances have improved our understanding of the biological mechanisms, expanded device options, and refined treatment strategies. However, the evidence also shows that safety, side effects, and long-term outcomes vary by modality, skin type, and treatment parameters. The most robust evidence supports combination therapy for melasma, broader pigment-targeted IPL, and LED-based photobiomodulation for skin rejuvenation, while the evidence for standalone whitening remains stronger in rejuvenation than in isolated brightening [N3-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1]. The field is advancing rapidly, but it remains an evidence-based area where careful patient selection, standardized protocols, and cautious application are essential [N5-F4][N3-F2].

A mini-report on safety, side effects, and clinical limitations

Overall, light-based aesthetic treatments—particularly IPL and lasers—are widely used but carry a mix of acute, long-term, and device-specific risks. The evidence suggests that these technologies are generally safe in routine clinical use, yet they are not without limitations, especially when misapplied or when patients have phototypes that increase vulnerability to adverse effects [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-F4][N5-R4].

Common acute adverse effects include redness, swelling, burns, blisters, and temporary skin discoloration. IPL and laser devices can overheat the skin if settings are improperly chosen, and this can result in burns or blisters that may scar [N5-R2][N5-R3][N7-R3][N7-R4]. In addition, IPL can cause reversible hyperpigmentation or, less commonly, permanent hypopigmentation, especially when parameters are mismatched for the patient’s skin color or ethnicity [N5-F4]. IPL-related oxidative stress and DNA damage have also been noted in the literature, though the evidence base suggests these effects are not clinically catastrophic and are generally less severe than those of ultraviolet radiation [N5-R5][N5-F4].

Longer-term concerns are more nuanced. Although lasers and IPL are not known to cause skin cancer, the long-term safety literature notes that they are not without long-term risks, and some studies have documented rare adverse events and DNA damage concerns [N5-F4]. The same review also notes that IPL can generate reactive oxidative species and DNA damage similar to UV exposure, though the wavelengths commonly used in IPL are generally above the short UV range that is most damaging to DNA [N5-R5][N5-F4]. A separate review on ocular safety found that some IPL goggles provided insufficient protection, which is an important safety concern for practitioners and patients [N7-R1]. This points to a broader limitation: device-specific safety depends on proper use, eye protection, and operator expertise.

Skin types and sensitivity concerns are especially important. IPL is generally considered versatile, but its broad-spectrum nature can make it less predictable in darker skin types. The literature explicitly warns that incorrect parameters can cause post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and that darker skin types are more at risk for PIH and other complications [N5-F4][N5-R1]. IPL devices can also make the skin more vulnerable to ultraviolet rays after treatment, intensifying sensitivity and increasing the risk of complications [N5-R1]. This sensitivity concern is reinforced by the fact that IPL and laser treatments can be used at home or in less regulated settings, where improper application is more common and risk is higher [N7-R3][N7-R4].

Evidence gaps and unmet clinical needs are clear. The safety literature is strong on acute adverse effects and some long-term concerns, but it remains thin on definitive long-term cancer risk, and the evidence base is still considered limited in some comparative studies [N5-F4]. The evidence also shows that treatment outcomes depend heavily on device type, wavelength selection, and patient characteristics, yet standardized protocols are not always uniformly adopted across studies or practices [N5-F4][N4-F3]. For clinical decision-making, safety outcomes in many studies are judged with low certainty, and this matters because side effects can outweigh aesthetic benefits in some cases [N3-F2]. The broader limitation is that while light-based therapies are popular and increasingly accessible, their real-world safety and long-term effects are still best supported by cautious, individualized application rather than one-size-fits-all protocols [N5-F4][N7-R1][N7-R4].

A mini-report on hyperpigmentation treatment and melasma-specific light-based strategies

Melasma is a chronic, relapsing hyperpigmentation disorder driven by complex interactions among genetic predisposition, hormonal fluctuations, sun exposure, and inflammation [N3-F2]. Age spots are also a broad category of hyperpigmentation, and while the evidence set is less specific to age spots than to melasma, light-based therapies are used clinically for pigmentation concerns, including signs of aging like age spots [N3-R2]. For melasma, the evidence strongly supports combination therapy with topical agents as a more effective strategy than monotherapy [N3-F2].

The best-supported modalities for melasma are laser and light-based therapies combined with topical agents. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials found that combination therapy improved melasma severity and patient satisfaction, with statistically significant improvements at 8, 12, and 16 weeks [N3-F2]. The study also found that combination therapy carried a higher risk of adverse events, mainly erythema and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and it concluded that careful patient selection and monitoring are crucial [N3-F2]. This is an important practical implication: melasma treatment is more effective when combined with topical agents, but the safety profile is more complex, especially because topical ingredients can also influence pigmentation and inflammation [N3-F2].

For age spots, the evidence is less specific than for melasma, but IPL and related light-based treatments are still used clinically for pigmentation and signs of aging [N3-R2]. The same review also notes that red light therapy is popular for skin concerns including signs of aging like wrinkles, age spots, and sagging skin [N3-R2]. However, the evidence for red light therapy as a standalone treatment for age spots is weaker than for combination melasma therapy, and the review emphasizes that the 2024 integrative review on photobiomodulation for melasma included nine relevant studies, suggesting that age spot treatment is not as well-established as melasma in the current evidence base [N3-R5][N3-F2].

Dose, frequency, and combination treatment patterns are important in both conditions. For melasma, combination therapy typically involves fractional laser treatment with topical medications [N3-F2]. The evidence indicates a cumulative therapeutic effect, with improvements starting to appear after 8 weeks and strengthening over time [N3-F2]. In practice, this suggests that treatment is often repeated and that protocols are not limited to a single session. The review also emphasizes that inconsistent treatment protocols, variations in laser parameters, and differences in skin phototypes and topical agents used have led to considerable heterogeneity in outcomes [N3-F2]. This heterogeneity supports the idea that standardized, protocol-driven approaches are needed to optimize results.

Limitations and risks specific to pigmentation disorders are substantial. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is a major concern, and the evidence shows that combination therapy can increase the risk of adverse events, including erythema and PIH [N3-F2]. The same review also reports that some studies showed minimal improvement or even worsening of melasma in darker skin types, especially due to PIH risks [N3-F2]. For age spots, the evidence set is less explicit on risks, but the broader IPL literature warns of reversible hyperpigmentation, permanent hypopigmentation, and skin sensitivity after treatment [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that IPL can make the skin more vulnerable to ultraviolet exposure and intensify sensitivity [N5-R1]. These limitations suggest that pigmentation disorders require cautious, individualized treatment with close monitoring.

In summary, for melasma, the best-supported strategy is laser/light-based therapy combined with topical agents; for age spots, light-based therapies are used clinically but the evidence is less robust than for melasma [N3-F2][N3-R2]. The most important treatment patterns are repeated sessions, combination with topical agents, and careful attention to skin phototype [N3-F2]. The main limitations are post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, PIH, skin sensitivity, and the need for standardized protocols [N3-F2][N5-F4].

A mini-report on current applications of laser, IPL, and LED in aesthetic medicine

Each modality is currently used for a distinct set of aesthetic indications, but their treatment protocols and parameters differ substantially. Laser, IPL, and LED all have broad roles in aesthetic dermatology, but lasers are often used for more targeted chromophore-specific treatments, IPL for broader pigmentation and vascular concerns, and LED for photobiomodulation-based skin rejuvenation and hair growth [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1][N3-R2].

For laser, the evidence emphasizes use in vascular and pigment-related conditions, with particular attention to fractional lasers and other laser systems used in melasma treatment [N3-F2]. The comparative IPL study in rosacea notes that pulsed dye laser, narrow-band IPL, and broad-band IPL are used for vascular concerns and that laser technologies can be tailored to individual patient needs and severity [N4-F3]. In skin rejuvenation, lasers are part of a broader treatment repertoire that includes topical agents, radiofrequency, injectables, and surgery [N1-F1]. In melasma, lasers are combined with topical agents to improve pigmentation and patient satisfaction [N3-F2].

IPL is widely used for skin rejuvenation and pigmentation concerns, including vascular and pigmented lesions. The evidence set shows that IPL is described as a “photo facial” for improving skin color and texture without surgery [N1-R4]. It is also used clinically for skin photoaging and laxity in Asian patients [N1-R5], and the evidence indicates that IPL is often configured for different emission spectra by varying light filtration [N5-F4]. The comparative IPL study in rosacea further explains that IPL delivers non-coherent, broad-spectrum light capable of addressing various dermatological concerns, including vascular lesions, and that narrow-band IPL can improve target specificity [N4-F3]. However, broad-band IPL can carry a higher risk of pigmentation changes, while narrow-band IPL is associated with fewer adverse effects [N4-F3]. This reflects a key protocol difference: IPL treatment parameters are adjusted by wavelength filtering and energy density to match the target condition and patient characteristics [N4-F3].

LED is increasingly used for skin rejuvenation and hair growth. The evidence set states that low-level light therapy and LED therapy have gained popularity in aesthetic dermatology for treating skin aging through photobiomodulation [N1-F1]. A study on a near-infrared LED device showed clinical efficacy in skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement, with improvements in wrinkle count, skin moisture, elasticity, and density after 12 weeks of treatment [N1-F1]. The same study used a broader spectral range and reported no adverse reactions, which suggests that LED can be used in a relatively safe manner in some settings [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that newer LED devices may have broader action spectra that can increase efficacy [N1-F1]. In contrast to lasers and IPL, LED devices are generally considered lower energy and less likely to produce burns or blisters, but their effects are usually slower and more cumulative [N1-F1][N4-R3].

Common indications across the modalities are skin rejuvenation, pigmentation concerns, vascular conditions, and hair growth. Laser is used for vascular and pigment-related conditions, melasma, and skin rejuvenation when combined with topical agents [N3-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1]. IPL is used for skin rejuvenation, pigmentation, vascular lesions, and hair removal [N1-R4][N1-R5][N4-F3]. LED is used for skin rejuvenation and hair growth enhancement [N1-F1]. For hair removal, the evidence set shows that diode lasers and IPL are both used, with diode lasers generally showing higher efficacy and better comfort in some studies [N8-R1][N8-R2][N8-R3]. This is important because it shows that the same modality can be used across different indications, but the choice of device depends on the condition, skin type, and desired outcome.

Treatment protocols and parameters differ across devices. Lasers are typically chosen for more targeted chromophore-specific treatments and can be adjusted by wavelength, pulse duration, and energy density [N4-F3]. IPL is configured by varying light filtration to target different chromophores and is often used with adjustable energy settings [N5-F4][N4-F3]. LED is generally delivered through photobiomodulation protocols that use specific wavelengths, such as red or near-infrared light, and may be applied continuously over a longer session [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that home-use IPL devices can have similar efficacy and safety to salon-based IPL devices, which reflects a broader trend toward consumer access but also underscores the importance of proper settings and supervision [N4-R2][N7-R3]. In clinical practice, contraindications include photosensitivity, inflammation, skin disorders, skin allergies, and pregnancy/breastfeeding [N1-F1]. For IPL and lasers, darker skin types are especially vulnerable to PIH, and incorrect parameters can cause burns, blisters, hypopigmentation, or hyperpigmentation [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a device-specific approach to treatment, with lasers for targeted vascular/pigment conditions, IPL for broader pigmentation and vascular concerns, and LED for photobiomodulation-based skin rejuvenation and hair growth [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F3].

A mini-report on recent scientific advances in light-based whitening and brightening

Recent scientific advances in light-based whitening and brightening have focused on broader biological targets and pathways beyond simple light delivery. The evidence set indicates that light-based therapies are increasingly understood not just as photothermal treatments but as photobiomodulation approaches that alter cellular activity, tissue regeneration, repair, and inflammation [N2-R1][N1-F1]. This broader mechanistic view supports the use of light for skin rejuvenation, hair growth, and pigmentation-related concerns [N1-F1][N2-R1].

New biological targets or pathways implicated in light-based whitening include the cellular and molecular mechanisms of photobiomodulation. The literature suggests that light can affect chromophores, influence cellular signaling pathways, and modulate inflammation and tissue repair [N2-R1][N1-F1]. For brightening, the evidence emphasizes that photobiomodulation can reduce inflammation and improve skin texture, which contributes to a brighter appearance [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The review on skin brightening and hyperpigmentation care also notes recent advances in hyperpigmentation care, suggesting that scientific research continues to refine the biological rationale for light-based brightening [N2-R3]. However, the evidence set is thinner on specific molecular targets for whitening than on general mechanisms, so the strongest supported pathway is photobiomodulation via chromophore absorption and downstream signaling [N2-R1][N1-F1].

Recent device or formulation improvements include broader spectral ranges and more targeted light delivery. A study on a new near-infrared LED device showed that a broader spectral range may enhance efficacy compared to conventional narrow-band NIR chips [N1-F1]. The same study used a device with a broader spectrum and reported significant clinical improvement in skin rejuvenation, including reductions in wrinkles and improvements in skin moisture, elasticity, and density [N1-F1]. This suggests that device innovation is moving toward wider action spectra to improve outcomes. The evidence also notes that newer LED devices may have enhanced utility, consistent with broader trends in aesthetic medical devices [N6-R4]. In addition, the literature indicates that IPL can be configured with different emission spectra and that narrow-band IPL can improve target specificity [N5-F4][N4-F3]. These advances reflect a shift toward more personalized and effective light delivery rather than broad, one-size-fits-all wavelengths.

Clinical evidence for efficacy and patient outcomes is positive but mixed in terms of strength. For skin rejuvenation, the nNIR LED study reported significant improvements in wrinkle count, skin moisture, elasticity, and density, with no adverse reactions reported [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that over 90% of patients reported some improvement after red light therapy, including softer and smoother skin, less redness, and lightening of dark spots [N2-R4]. This supports the clinical relevance of light-based therapies for brightening and aging signs. However, the evidence base for red light therapy is less robust than for combination melasma therapy, and the review emphasizes that patient-reported outcomes can be encouraging even when the literature is still evolving [N2-R4][N2-R1].
